prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I moved from my opening first place, dynamical mean-field theory (B043), to the optical lattice clock after reading the other seven ballots. B013 is the only shortlisted entry ranked by all eight members, and seven of us placed it in the top three. That breadth matters because the members came from different subfields and weighed credit and maturity differently. The science is clean. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift on the clock transition, so many atoms can be interrogated in a lattice. Ye's group then carried the strontium clock to roughly 10^-18 stability and accuracy. Independent laboratories with strontium and ytterbium reproduce the performance, and the instruments feed directly into tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the planned redefinition of the second. Two names give the cleanest attribution of any entry on the shortlist: the concept and early demonstration, and the record-setting realization. The condensed-matter and electronic-structure candidates I know best all carry a credit gap or a timing question that B013 does not.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (ion control) already honoured the lineage, so some may see lattice clocks as an excellent refinement rather than a new discovery. Precision metrology is also engineering-heavy, and the practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. Parallel claims by ion-clock groups and by European lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Sterr) are outside the supplied credit. I also note that my own preferred candidate, DMFT, would be the better fit to my expertise, but it has the weakest backing in this room (only my ballot ranked it), and I do not treat my own opening enthusiasm as evidence of broader merit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first, argues the two-person attribution is natural and that the 2005 comb prize makes it a timely continuation, and discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory with Ye associated with that group.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case, but I would not lean on Kroll's argument that the 2005 prize makes this timely, because the same fact is the best argument against novelty. The better reason is that lattice clocks introduced a new idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms) that the comb and ion-clock work did not contain. Kroll's disclosure is a perceived tie, not a documented conflict, and it is exactly what the committee should record. Since B013 has strong support from members with no such tie (Danielsson, Johansson, Mehlig, Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce), his transparency does not change the balance.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B001 first with Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, admits the choice of three from four names is a judgement call that omits Virdee, and discloses a close link to circuit QED (B054) through Chalmers and WACQT.
responses.response: I respect the Higgs experimental discovery as the most consequential result on the list, and I ranked it fifth only because of attribution. This is a serious disagreement with the way the Higgs ballots are being treated. The seven of us who ranked B001 name three different trios (Danielsson and Kroll drop Della Negra, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson drop Virdee, and Pearce and I dropped Jenni), which suggests the credited set is arbitrary and that a prize for collaboration leaders would draw lasting dispute over who was left out. I would not trade a clean attribution for the larger headline. I also welcome Johansson's candour about B054 and agree it should sit with the recusal question rather than be argued on merit by him.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs first and puts the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator entry third, calling it a prediction followed by a clean experimental realization and noting the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission as a significant weakness.
responses.response: I share the third place for B044, and it is my first fallback because band-structure calculations were essential to identify real materials. I also share the BHZ concern, and I would go further than Danielsson: the HgTe route was proposed by BHZ, so a prize built on the supplied trio credits the experiment without crediting the specific prediction that motivated it. That is why I keep B044 as an alternative rather than my preferred option, and why the 2016 overlap needs a clear citation that separates the Z2 invariant and the helical edge state from the earlier topological phase-transition work.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second with only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, arguing the prediction and experiment are clearly separable and that Bistritzer's allocation is the unresolved point.
responses.response: Her atomic-structure reading of the clock reinforces my view that the physics is understood in detail. On B046 I agree that the theory-and-experiment pair is clean but I differ on timing: with the superconducting mechanism still debated and the field only about eight years old, I would wait. The scientific interest is real, since continuum and ab initio descriptions of moire bands matter to my own field, but I would not let that pull the prize forward.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see optical lattice clocks as a new achievement or as a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the redefinition of the second will have taken place, or be firmly scheduled, by the time of the decision.
Priority and credit between Katori's proposal, Ye's realizations and the other lattice-clock groups, which I recall from general knowledge rather than from verified sources.

Whether B043 (Georges, Vollhardt, Kotliar) can attract support beyond my own ballot once the discovery-versus-method question is discussed, and whether Metzner's omission from the credited names makes it unworkable.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict with the preferred candidate is apparent from my provided profile. My documented connections (Uppsala Materials Theory, my doctoral supervisor Borje Johansson, Los Alamos, co-authors of my books) do not involve the credited names. I note a subject-matter closeness to B043 (DMFT and DFT+DMFT) and to the electronic-structure side of B044 and B046, but no personal link to the credited candidates, and I discount my opening support for B043 accordingly.
